# Nine questions, one toolkit {.divider background-color="#008CB7"}

[Act I · The tension]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Welcome to the chapter that pulls the whole book together. Every case study uses the same estimator (OLS, and in 13.8 its IV cousin) on a different real dataset. What changes from case to case is the question, the data structure, the standard errors, and — above all — the source of variation that lets us interpret a slope.
:::

## Regression describes — but can it explain *why*?

By now we can fit a line, add controls, and read a slope. But a slope is an **association**: schools with better-educated parents score higher; countries with stronger property rights are richer. Does the regressor *cause* the outcome?

. . .

This chapter works through **nine case studies** on real data. The first four push observational regression as far as it goes. The last four bring in a **research design** (an RCT, difference-in-differences, a regression discontinuity, or an instrumental variable) that turns a slope into a **causal** claim.

[The question running through every case is the same: *where does the variation in the regressor come from?*]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Frame the deck as a climb: describe → specify → diagnose bias → design for causation. Each case is self-contained, with its own data, code, output and interpretation, so you can teach any case on its own. Use the agenda on the next slide to jump.
:::

## The climb: from description to causation

::: {.incremental}
- **Describe** (13.1, 13.4): conditional associations, with controls and honest SEs
- **Impose structure** (13.2): a theory-based functional form makes the coefficients interpretable as elasticities and gives a testable restriction
- **Diagnose bias** (13.3): the omitted-variables formula tells us *how much* a missing regressor distorts a slope
- **Design for causation** (13.5–13.8): an RCT, DiD, RD or IV builds a **credible counterfactual**
:::

[Controls can only close the confounders we *measure*. A design closes the ones we don't.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The ladder idea: each rung adds an assumption that is easier to defend. Description makes no causal claim. Structure adds theory. The OVB formula tells us the direction and size of bias. Designs replace "I controlled for everything" (unverifiable) with a specific, defensible identifying assumption: random assignment, parallel trends, continuity at a cutoff, or an exclusion restriction.
:::

## One estimator, three ways to be honest about uncertainty {.smaller}

| SE type | pyfixest syntax | Use when errors are… | Cases |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Heteroskedasticity-robust | `vcov="HC1"` | independent, unequal variance (cross-sections) | 13.1, 13.7, 13.8 |
| HAC (Newey–West) | `vcov="NW"` + `time_id`, `lag` | autocorrelated over time (time series) | 13.2, 13.3 |
| Cluster-robust | `vcov={"CRV1": "group"}` | correlated within groups | 13.4 (maker), 13.5 (family), 13.6 (community) |

[The coefficient is identical under all three. Only the standard errors, and therefore the $t$-statistics, $p$-values and confidence intervals, change.]{.comment}

[Match the standard error to how the data were generated. In 13.4, clustering makes the SEs 6–9× larger than HC1.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter uses one estimation function, pf.feols, throughout. The vcov argument changes only the inference. HC1 handles heteroskedasticity across independent observations. Newey–West (HAC) also allows correlation between nearby time periods — the chapter uses 3 lags for the 24-year Cobb–Douglas series and 5 lags for the 45-year post-1970 Phillips series. CRV1 allows arbitrary correlation inside each cluster (manufacturer, family, community). We will see in 13.4 that this choice is not cosmetic.
:::

## Five ideas anchor this chapter

::: {.incremental}
- **Production function**: inputs $\to$ output. Cobb–Douglas $Q = AK^{\beta_2}L^{\beta_3}$ is linear in logs
- **Constant returns to scale**: doubling every input doubles output, i.e. $\beta_2 + \beta_3 = 1$
- **Selection bias**: treated and untreated units differ *before* treatment; random assignment removes the difference
- **Parallel trends**: the DiD assumption that, without treatment, both groups would have moved together
- **Counterfactual**: the unobserved "what would have happened"; every design imputes it differently
:::

[A credible causal estimate is not a better regression. It is a better *source of variation*.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These are the chapter's Key Concepts. Production function and CRS anchor 13.2; selection bias anchors 13.5; parallel trends anchors 13.6; the counterfactual idea ties 13.5–13.8 together.
:::

# Act II-a · Observational regression, pushed to its limits {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Cases 13.1–13.4 · describe, structure, diagnose]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Four cases with observational data. None claims causality in the strict sense; each teaches a tool: controls and multicollinearity (13.1), logs and testing a restriction (13.2), the OVB formula (13.3), and clustering (13.4).
:::

# Case 13.1 · What drives school performance? {#case-131 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Multiple regression · cross-section · HC1 standard errors]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case 13.1: the California Academic Performance Index. Tools: bivariate vs multiple regression, correlation matrix, multicollinearity, reading partial effects.
:::

## The question: family background or school resources? {.smaller}

**Data.** 807 California high schools, 1999 (`AED_API99.DTA`). The **Academic Performance Index (API)** runs from 200 to 1000; the state target is 800.

| Variable | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `api99` | Academic Performance Index, 1999 (outcome) |
| `edparent` | average parent education, in years |
| `meals` | % of students in the free / reduced-price lunch program (poverty proxy) |
| `englearn` | % English learners |
| `yearround` | 1 if the school runs a multi-track year-round calendar |
| `credteach`, `emerteach` | % of teachers with full / emergency credentials |

[Every regressor is the result of choices by families, districts or teachers, so expect **associations**, not causal effects.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Economic question: what determines school performance, resources (teachers) or demographics (parents' education, poverty, language)? Nothing here is randomly assigned. Families choose where to live, teachers sort across schools, districts pick calendars. Keep that in mind for the interpretation.
:::

## Most schools fall well short of the 800 target

![Distribution of 1999 API scores across 807 high schools. Red: mean (620.9); green: the state target of 800.](figures/fig_api_hist.png)

[The mean school scores about 621, and only 4.8% of schools reach 800, so the outcome varies enough to explain.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Roughly symmetric (skewness ≈ 0.12, very slightly right-skewed). Scores range from below 400 to above 900. Mean 620.9. Only 4.8% of schools have API ≥ 800 (computed from the same data). Lots of variation to explain.
:::

## Code: load the data and fit the bivariate regression

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6|7-8|9-10"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                    # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                       # OLS / IV with R-style formulas
# 807 California high schools, 1999
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_API99.DTA"
data_api = pd.read_stata(url)               # read the Stata file into a DataFrame
vars_api = ["api99", "edparent", "meals", "englearn", "yearround", "credteach", "emerteach"]
data_api[vars_api].describe()               # summary statistics for the 7 variables
fit_api_biv = pf.feols("api99 ~ edparent", data=data_api, vcov="HC1")  # bivariate OLS
fit_api_biv.summary()                       # intercept, slope, robust SE, R²
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained: paste into an empty Colab cell. vcov="HC1" requests heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, appropriate for a cross-section of independent schools.
:::

## Output: one predictor explains 83.5% of the variation {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
| | Coef. | SE | $t$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Intercept | −400.314 | 15.993 | −25.03 |
| `edparent` | [79.529]{.key} | 1.219 | 65.25 |

[N = 807 · HC1 SEs · $R^2 = 0.835$ · 95% CI for slope: [77.14, 81.92]]{.comment}

Each additional year of average parent education is associated with **79.5 more API points**.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![API vs parent education, with the OLS line.](figures/fig_api_scatter.png)
:::
::::

[A huge, precise slope, but `edparent` also stands in for income, language and neighbourhood. Next, we add controls.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Estimated equation: API = −400.3 + 79.5 × edparent. R² = 0.835, which is unusually high for a cross-section. The intercept is an extrapolation (zero years of education is outside the data, which run from 9.6 to 16 years) and has no meaning on its own. The bivariate slope bundles everything correlated with parent education.
:::

## Code: are the regressors themselves correlated?

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-5|6-7"}
# continues from the previous block (data_api, vars_api already defined)
import seaborn as sns                       # statistical plotting (heatmap)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt             # figure handling
corr_matrix = data_api[vars_api].corr()     # pairwise Pearson correlations
print(corr_matrix.round(2))                 # numeric matrix, 2 decimals
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="coolwarm", center=0)  # coloured matrix
plt.show()                                  # display the heatmap
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

[Before adding controls, check how strongly they move together. That decides how precisely their separate effects can be estimated.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A correlation matrix is the quickest multicollinearity diagnostic. Strongly correlated regressors carry overlapping information, so OLS has little independent variation left to tell their effects apart.
:::

## Output: the regressors are strongly correlated {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Correlation matrix of API and its six candidate determinants.](figures/fig_corr_matrix.png){height="440"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
| Pair | $r$ |
|:--|--:|
| `api99`–`edparent` | [0.91]{.key} |
| `api99`–`englearn` | −0.66 |
| `api99`–`meals` | −0.54 |
| `edparent`–`englearn` | −0.71 |
| `edparent`–`meals` | −0.60 |
| `credteach`–`emerteach` | −0.82 |
:::
::::

[Parent education, poverty and English learners largely describe the *same* schools, so their separate effects will be hard to pull apart.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Strong negative correlations of API with meals (−0.54) and englearn (−0.66); strong positive with edparent (0.91). Among regressors: edparent–englearn −0.71, edparent–meals −0.60, and the two teacher-credential variables −0.82, which are nearly mirror images. Expect inflated standard errors on whichever of these overlapping variables carries less unique information.
:::

## Code: the multiple regression

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-10"}
# continues from the previous block
fit_api_mult = pf.feols("api99 ~ edparent + meals + englearn + yearround + credteach + emerteach",
                        data=data_api, vcov="HC1")   # six regressors, robust SEs
fit_api_mult.summary()                               # full coefficient table
coef_df = pd.DataFrame({                             # compact table of results
    "Coefficient": fit_api_mult.coef(),              # point estimates
    "Std Error": fit_api_mult.se(),                  # HC1 standard errors
    "t-stat": fit_api_mult.tstat(),                  # coefficient / SE
    "p-value": fit_api_mult.pvalue()                 # two-sided p-values
}).round(3)
print(coef_df)
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Same data, six regressors. Each coefficient is now a partial effect: the association with API holding the other five regressors fixed.
:::

## Output: parent education survives every control {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Intercept | −345.328 | 44.027 | −7.84 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [−431.75,&nbsp;−258.91] |
| `edparent` | [73.942]{.key} | 1.835 | 40.29 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [70.34,&nbsp;77.54] |
| `meals` | 0.079 | 0.092 | 0.86 | 0.390 | [−0.10,&nbsp;0.26] |
| `englearn` | −0.358 | 0.177 | −2.02 | 0.044 | [−0.71,&nbsp;−0.01] |
| `yearround` | 25.956 | 10.752 | 2.41 | 0.016 | [4.85,&nbsp;47.06] |
| `credteach` | 0.387 | 0.349 | 1.11 | 0.268 | [−0.30,&nbsp;1.07] |
| `emerteach` | −1.470 | 0.358 | −4.11 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [−2.17,&nbsp;−0.77] |

[N = 807 · HC1 SEs · $R^2 = 0.853$ (vs 0.835 with `edparent` alone)]{.comment}

[With five controls, the parent-education slope falls only from 79.5 to 73.9, and the controls add just 1.8 points of $R^2$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.1: the parent-education coefficient stays around 74 points even after controlling for meals, English learners, year-round calendars and teacher credentials. The jump in R² is small because edparent already captures most of what the other variables measure.
:::

## Reading the coefficients (1): what "holding constant" means

::: {.incremental}
- **`edparent` 73.9**: comparing schools with the *same* poverty, language, calendar and credential mix, one more year of parent education goes with 73.9 more API points
- **`meals` 0.08 ($p = 0.39$)**: on its own, poverty correlates $-0.54$ with API, but once parent education is held fixed it adds **no separate** predictive information
- That does **not** mean poverty is irrelevant: it overlaps heavily with `edparent` ($r = -0.60$), so the data cannot separate the two
:::

[A partial effect answers "compared with otherwise-similar schools…", and the answer depends on which variables we hold fixed.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Interpret each coefficient as a comparison between schools that are alike on every other regressor. An insignificant coefficient on a highly collinear variable (meals) says "no detectable separate association given the others", not "zero effect".
:::

## Reading the coefficients (2): collinearity and sign changes

::: {.incremental}
- **`emerteach` −1.47 per percentage point**: more emergency-credentialed teachers, lower scores ($p < 0.001$)
- Its mirror image **`credteach`** is insignificant ($p = 0.27$): the two are correlated $-0.82$, so they compete for the same variation
- **`yearround` +26.0** ($p = 0.016$): year-round schools score 26 points *higher* conditional on the rest, although the simple correlation is negative ($-0.19$)
:::

[Collinear regressors share credit unpredictably, and conditioning can flip a sign, which previews the omitted-variables lesson of 13.3.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
credteach and emerteach nearly mirror each other (fully credentialed vs emergency credentials), so whichever enters with more unique variation absorbs the effect. The yearround sign change is a small preview of 13.3: what you condition on changes the slope.
:::

## Why these are associations, not causal effects

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What the regression holds fixed
- the six measured characteristics
- nothing else
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What it cannot hold fixed
- family income, home resources, private tutoring
- which families *choose* which districts
- how teachers *sort* toward easier schools
:::
::::

[`edparent` is a proxy for a whole bundle of advantages, so 73.9 is a conditional association, not "the effect of sending parents back to school".]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Standard caveat for observational regression: omitted variables correlated with both edparent and API (income, wealth, neighbourhood) load onto the edparent coefficient. Selection of families into districts and of teachers into schools also breaks any causal reading. The chapter notes California's "similar schools" index, which uses exactly this kind of regression to benchmark schools against comparable peers: a descriptive use for which conditional associations are fine.
:::

# Case 13.2 · Does doubling inputs double output? {#case-132 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Cobb–Douglas production function · log-log model · HAC standard errors]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case 13.2: Douglas's U.S. manufacturing data, 1899–1922. Tools: log transformation, elasticities, a test of a linear restriction, retransformation of log predictions, HAC standard errors for time series.
:::

## The question: returns to scale in U.S. manufacturing {.smaller}

The **Cobb–Douglas** production function maps capital $K$ and labor $L$ into output $Q$:

$$Q = A\,K^{\beta_2}\,L^{\beta_3}$$

| If $\beta_2 + \beta_3$ is… | Returns to scale | Doubling both inputs… |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $= 1$ | constant | doubles output |
| $> 1$ | increasing | more than doubles output |
| $< 1$ | decreasing | less than doubles output |

[Returns to scale come down to a *single number*, $\beta_2 + \beta_3$, which we can estimate and test.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
A is total factor productivity (the technology level). β₂ and β₃ are the output elasticities of capital and labor. Scaling both inputs by λ multiplies output by λ^(β₂+β₃), which is why the sum decides returns to scale. Competitive-market theory often predicts constant returns.
:::

## Taking logs turns a multiplicative model into a linear regression

$$\ln Q = \underbrace{\ln A}_{\beta_1} + \beta_2 \ln K + \beta_3 \ln L + u$$

[The model is now linear in its parameters, so OLS applies. Each slope is an **elasticity**: $\beta_2 = \partial \ln Q / \partial \ln K$, the percentage change in output per 1% change in capital, holding labor fixed.]{.comment}

[Logs do two jobs here: they make the model estimable by OLS, and they make the coefficients unit-free elasticities.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.2. Because both sides are in logs, a coefficient measures a proportional response. Strictly, "a 1% change in K changes Q by β₂%" is a marginal (calculus) statement; for finite changes it is an approximation that is excellent for small changes.
:::

## The data: 24 years of output, capital and labor (1899 = 100) {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
| Index in 1922 | Value | Growth since 1899 |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Output $Q$ | 240 | 2.4× |
| Capital $K$ | 431 | [4.3×]{.key} |
| Labor $L$ | 161 | 1.6× |
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why HAC standard errors?**

- **Time series**: booms, recessions and technology shocks persist, so errors are **autocorrelated**
- Volatility differs across periods (e.g. World War I), so errors are **heteroskedastic**
- Newey–West (HAC) SEs allow for both; the chapter uses **3 lags**
:::
::::

[Capital grew much faster than output or labor. How the regression splits output growth between the two inputs is the elasticity question.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Douglas (1976) data; all series are indices with 1899 = 100. Default OLS SEs assume uncorrelated, homoskedastic errors, which is wrong here. HC1 fixes heteroskedasticity but ignores autocorrelation. HAC (heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent) SEs fix both. With only 24 observations, even HAC SEs are themselves imprecise.
:::

## Code: log-transform and estimate with Newey–West SEs

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-7|8-10|11-13"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                    # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import numpy as np                          # np.log for the transform
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                       # OLS with R-style formulas
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_COBBDOUGLAS.DTA"
data_cobb = pd.read_stata(url)              # 24 years of U.S. manufacturing, 1899–1922
data_cobb["lnq"] = np.log(data_cobb["q"])   # log output
data_cobb["lnk"] = np.log(data_cobb["k"])   # log capital
data_cobb["lnl"] = np.log(data_cobb["l"])   # log labor
data_cobb["_time"] = range(len(data_cobb))  # time index required by Newey–West
fit_cobb = pf.feols("lnq ~ lnk + lnl", data=data_cobb,
                    vcov="NW", vcov_kwargs={"time_id": "_time", "lag": 3})  # HAC SEs, 3 lags
fit_cobb.summary()                          # elasticities, HAC SEs, R²
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. Note vcov="NW" with a time index and lag = 3. This is the chapter's specification; plain OLS SEs would ignore the autocorrelation in this time series.
:::

## Output: labor's elasticity is about 3.5× capital's {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | HAC SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Intercept | −0.177 | 0.398 | −0.45 | 0.660 | [−1.000,&nbsp;0.646] |
| `lnk` (capital) | [0.233]{.key} | 0.063 | 3.72 | 0.001 | [0.103,&nbsp;0.363] |
| `lnl` (labor) | [0.807]{.key} | 0.135 | 6.00 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.529,&nbsp;1.086] |

[N = 24 · Newey–West SEs, 3 lags · $R^2 = 0.957$]{.comment}

::: {.incremental}
- Holding labor fixed, a 1% increase in capital is associated with **≈ 0.23%** more output
- Holding capital fixed, a 1% increase in labor is associated with **≈ 0.81%** more output
:::

[Early-1900s manufacturing was labor-driven: the labor elasticity (0.81) is about 3.5 times the capital elasticity (0.23).]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Estimated equation: ln Q = −0.177 + 0.233 ln K + 0.807 ln L. The "≈" matters: elasticities describe small proportional changes; for a large change, compute (1+Δ)^β − 1 instead. Labor/capital ratio of elasticities: 0.807 / 0.233 ≈ 3.46. The very high R² partly reflects that all three series trend upward together (see the caveats slide).
:::

## Code: test constant returns with the HAC covariance matrix

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-2|3-6|7-9"}
# continues from the previous block
from scipy import stats                     # F distribution for the p-value
R = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 1.0])               # restriction vector: picks out β_K + β_L
b_hat = fit_cobb.coef().values              # coefficients [Intercept, lnk, lnl]
V_hac = fit_cobb._vcov                      # Newey–West (HAC) covariance matrix
df_resid = fit_cobb._N - len(b_hat)         # residual degrees of freedom: 24 − 3 = 21
f_stat = (R @ b_hat - 1.0)**2 / (R @ V_hac @ R)   # Wald statistic for H0: β_K + β_L = 1
p_value = 1 - stats.f.cdf(f_stat, 1, df_resid)    # p-value from F(1, 21)
print(R @ b_hat, f_stat, p_value)           # estimated sum, F, p
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

[The test reuses the HAC covariance matrix, so the inference matches the HAC standard errors on the previous slide.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.3: a test of one linear restriction on two coefficients. A classical restricted-vs-unrestricted F test would assume iid errors, which we have already argued against; the Wald form with V_HAC is robust. R·b̂ is the estimated sum; R·V·Rᵀ is its variance.
:::

## Output: the data are consistent with constant returns to scale {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Quantity | Value |
|:--|--:|
| $\hat\beta_K + \hat\beta_L$ | [1.040]{.key} |
| HAC SE of the sum | 0.084 |
| $F(1, 21)$ | 0.23 |
| $p$-value | [0.636]{.key} |
| 95% CI for the sum | [0.87,&nbsp;1.21] |
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
- $H_0: \beta_K + \beta_L = 1$ is **not rejected** at any conventional level
- But the 95% interval spans **0.87 to 1.21**: mild decreasing *or* increasing returns also fit the data
- "Fail to reject" is not "prove". With 24 years, the test has limited power
:::
::::

[The estimate (1.04) is close to 1 and statistically indistinguishable from it, which supports constant returns without proving them.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter reports F = 0.23 and p = 0.636. The 95% CI uses the same HAC SE (0.084) and t(21) = 2.08: 1.040 ± 2.08 × 0.084 ≈ [0.87, 1.21]. This interval is derived arithmetic from the chapter's output, not a new estimate. Present the result honestly: the evidence is consistent with CRS, and also consistent with modest departures from it.
:::

## The fitted model tracks output across 24 years

![Actual vs predicted output, 1899–1922. Predictions are $e^{\widehat{\ln Q}}$ multiplied by the retransformation factor $e^{\hat\sigma^2/2}$.](figures/fig_x_04.png)

[To predict *levels* from a log model, exponentiate **and** rescale by $e^{\hat\sigma^2/2}$; here $\hat\sigma = 0.058$, so the correction is tiny (×1.0017).]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Code (in the chapter): se = sqrt(Σû² / (N − k)); q_pred = exp(se²/2) · exp(fitted ln Q). Because E[e^u] = e^(σ²/2) > 1 for normal errors, simply exponentiating fitted logs under-predicts the mean level. Here σ̂ = 0.058, so the factor is 1.0017. The predicted series follows actual output closely, with the largest misses in the 1920–22 swings.
:::

## Caveats: why 24 trending observations call for humility

::: {.incremental}
- **Trending series**: $Q$, $K$ and $L$ all rise over time, so part of the $R^2 = 0.957$ is a shared trend, not a production relationship (the spurious-regression worry)
- **Technology held constant**: $A$ is a single constant; omitted technical progress that grew with capital would load onto $\hat\beta_K$
- **Small sample**: 24 points, and HAC SEs are themselves noisy with so few years
- **Aggregation**: one "representative" manufacturing sector stands in for many industries
:::

[The CRS test is informative, but treat the separate elasticities as fragile.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
These are standard caveats for an aggregate time-series production function, not results the chapter computes. The spurious-regression problem (regressing one trending series on another) is covered in time-series chapters. A natural extension would add a time trend to proxy technical change; this deck does not estimate it.
:::

# Case 13.3 · Why did the Phillips curve break? {#case-133 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Omitted variables bias · time series · HAC standard errors]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case 13.3: the most important *diagnostic* case in the chapter. The same two variables give opposite slopes in two periods; the omitted-variables-bias formula explains exactly why.
:::

## The question: is there a stable unemployment–inflation trade-off?

::: {.incremental}
- **Phillips (1958)**: lower unemployment went with higher wage inflation, so policymakers saw a *menu*: choose a point on the curve
- **1970s stagflation**: high unemployment *and* high inflation together, and the menu fell apart
- **Friedman–Phelps**: the curve shifts with **expected inflation**; leave expectations out and the curve is misspecified
:::

$$\text{Inflation}_t = \beta_1 + \beta_2\,\text{Urate}_t + \beta_3\,\text{ExpInflation}_t + u_t$$

[If expected inflation belongs in the model, omitting it is not harmless. It can distort, even reverse, the unemployment slope.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Data: AED_PHILLIPS.DTA, U.S. 1949–2014 (66 years). inflgdp = annual inflation from the GDP deflator (%); urate = civilian unemployment rate (%); inflgdp1yr = one-year-ahead expected inflation from the Survey of Professional Forecasters. In this dataset the expectations series is available only from 1970 onward, so the augmented model can only be run post-1970.
:::

## Code: the pre-1970 Phillips curve

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-5|6-9|10"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                    # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                       # OLS with R-style formulas
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_PHILLIPS.DTA"
data_phillips = pd.read_stata(url)          # U.S. annual data, 1949–2014
data_pre1970 = data_phillips[data_phillips["year"] < 1970].copy()   # 1949–1969
data_pre1970["_time"] = range(len(data_pre1970))                    # time index for HAC
fit_pre = pf.feols("inflgdp ~ urate", data=data_pre1970,
                   vcov="NW", vcov_kwargs={"time_id": "_time", "lag": 3})  # HAC, 3 lags
fit_pre.summary()                           # slope on unemployment
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. 21 annual observations, 1949–1969, Newey–West SEs with 3 lags.
:::

## Output: before 1970, the trade-off is there {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
| | Coef. | HAC SE | $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Intercept | 7.106 | 1.581 | <&nbsp;0.001 |
| `urate` | [−1.030]{.key} | 0.325 | 0.005 |

[N = 21 (1949–1969) · NW, 3 lags · $R^2 = 0.454$]{.comment}

One **percentage point** more unemployment is associated with about **1.03 percentage points** less inflation.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![1949–1969: inflation vs unemployment, with the OLS line.](figures/fig_phillips_pre.png)
:::
::::

[The classic downward-sloping Phillips curve: negative and statistically significant ($p = 0.005$).]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Both variables are measured in percent, so the slope is in percentage points per percentage point, not "1%" in the proportional sense. The chapter's explanation for why the simple curve worked then: expected inflation was low and stable in the 1950s–60s, so omitting it did little damage. (This dataset cannot check that directly, because the SPF expectations series starts in 1970.)
:::

## Code: the same regression after 1970

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6"}
# continues from the previous block
data_post1970 = data_phillips[data_phillips["year"] >= 1970].copy()  # 1970–2014
data_post1970["_time"] = range(len(data_post1970))                   # time index for HAC
fit_post = pf.feols("inflgdp ~ urate", data=data_post1970,
                    vcov="NW", vcov_kwargs={"time_id": "_time", "lag": 5})  # HAC, 5 lags
fit_post.summary()                          # has the slope survived?
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

[The specification is identical. Only the period changes, and with it the lag length for the longer series.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
45 annual observations, 1970–2014; the chapter uses 5 Newey–West lags for the longer series.
:::

## Output: after 1970, the slope flips sign {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
| | Coef. | HAC SE | $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Intercept | 1.928 | 1.868 | 0.308 |
| `urate` | [+0.265]{.key} | 0.326 | 0.420 |

[N = 45 (1970–2014) · NW, 5 lags · $R^2 = 0.028$]{.comment}

The point estimate is now **positive**, but it is **not significant** ($p = 0.42$), and $R^2$ collapses from 0.45 to 0.03.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![1970–2014: the fitted line now slopes upward, with far more scatter.](figures/fig_phillips_post.png)
:::
::::

[Same two variables, opposite sign. Either the economy changed, or the bivariate model was always missing something.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.4. Be precise: the slope flips sign, but we cannot reject a zero relationship (95% CI from −0.39 to +0.92). Stagflation shows up as points with high unemployment and high inflation. The Friedman–Phelps answer: the missing piece is expected inflation.
:::

## The OVB formula: what an omitted regressor does to a slope

$$\underbrace{y = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x + \beta_3 z + u}_{\text{long (true) model}} \qquad \underbrace{z = \gamma_1 + \gamma\,x + v}_{\text{auxiliary regression}}$$

. . .

Substitute $z$ into the long model and regress $y$ on $x$ alone:

$$E[b_2] = \beta_2 + \underbrace{\beta_3\,\gamma}_{\text{omitted variables bias}}$$

[The bias is (effect of the omitted $z$ on $y$) × (how $z$ moves with the included $x$). It vanishes only if $\beta_3 = 0$ **or** $\gamma = 0$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.5. Direction of the bias: sign(β₃) × sign(γ). If z raises y (β₃ > 0) and rises with x (γ > 0), the short slope is biased upward, and enough upward bias can turn a negative true slope positive. With OLS on the same sample, the in-sample version b₂(short) = β̂₂ + β̂₃·γ̂ holds exactly, not just in expectation.
:::

## Code: add expected inflation, then run the auxiliary regression

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-4|5-6|7-9|10"}
# continues from the previous block
data_exp = data_post1970.dropna(subset=["inflgdp1yr"]).copy()  # rows with expected inflation
data_exp["_time"] = range(len(data_exp))                       # time index for HAC
fit_augmented = pf.feols("inflgdp ~ urate + inflgdp1yr", data=data_exp,
                         vcov="NW", vcov_kwargs={"time_id": "_time", "lag": 5})  # long model
fit_aux = pf.feols("inflgdp1yr ~ urate", data=data_exp)        # auxiliary: z on x
beta2 = fit_augmented.coef()["urate"]       # true slope on unemployment
beta3 = fit_augmented.coef()["inflgdp1yr"]  # effect of expected inflation
gamma = fit_aux.coef()["urate"]             # how expectations co-move with unemployment
print(beta2 + beta3 * gamma, fit_post.coef()["urate"])  # predicted vs actual short slope
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
inflgdp1yr is one-year-ahead expected inflation from the Survey of Professional Forecasters. It is available for all 45 post-1970 years, so the long, short and auxiliary regressions use the same sample, which is what makes the decomposition exact.
:::

## Output: control for expectations and the negative slope returns {.smaller}

| Variable (long model) | Coef. | HAC SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:----------------------|------:|------:|----:|----:|:-------------|
| Intercept | 0.270 | 0.634 | 0.43 | 0.672 | [−1.01,&nbsp;1.55] |
| `urate` ($\hat\beta_2$) | [−0.128]{.key} | 0.081 | −1.58 | 0.122 | [−0.29,&nbsp;0.04] |
| `inflgdp1yr` ($\hat\beta_3$) | [1.146]{.key} | 0.085 | 13.48 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.97,&nbsp;1.32] |

[N = 45 · NW, 5 lags · $R^2 = 0.881$ · Auxiliary regression: $\hat\gamma = 0.343$ (SE 0.195, $p = 0.086$, default SEs)]{.comment}

[Expected inflation does most of the work ($R^2$ jumps from 0.03 to 0.88), and the unemployment slope turns negative again.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
β̂₃ ≈ 1.15: actual inflation moves roughly one-for-one with expected inflation (the chapter's "coefficient ≈ 1"; we have not formally tested β₃ = 1). β̂₂ = −0.128 has the Phillips-curve sign but is not significant at 5% (p = 0.12), so the trade-off is restored in sign, not firmly established. γ̂ = 0.343: years with higher unemployment also had higher expected inflation.
:::

## The OVB arithmetic explains the sign reversal exactly {.smaller}

$$b_2^{\text{short}} = \hat\beta_2 + \hat\beta_3\,\hat\gamma = -0.128 + 1.146 \times 0.343 = +0.265$$

| Piece | Value | Meaning |
|:--|--:|:--|
| $\hat\beta_2$ | −0.128 | unemployment slope, holding expectations fixed |
| $\hat\beta_3\hat\gamma$ | [+0.393]{.key} | bias from omitting expected inflation |
| $b_2^{\text{short}}$ | +0.265 | the bivariate post-1970 slope: an exact match |

[The bivariate slope gave unemployment credit for expected inflation's effect. The bias (+0.39) was large enough to flip the sign.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter calls this a "perfect match". It is perfect by construction: for OLS on a common sample the decomposition is an algebraic identity. Its value is in *attributing* the short slope: −0.128 of genuine trade-off plus +0.393 of omitted-variable bias. Economic story: 1970s supply shocks (oil) raised unemployment and inflation expectations together, so γ > 0; and expectations push inflation up (β₃ > 0); so the bias is positive.
:::

## Caveats: the trade-off is restored in sign, not proven

::: {.incremental}
- **Imprecision**: the augmented slope ($-0.128$, $p = 0.12$) and $\hat\gamma$ ($p = 0.086$) are not significant at 5%
- **Measurement**: expected inflation is a *forecasters' survey*, a proxy for what wage- and price-setters actually expected
- **Simultaneity**: inflation and unemployment are both outcomes of the same shocks and policies, so this is not a causal structural equation
- **Other omitted variables**: supply shocks and policy regimes can still bias the long model
:::

[The OVB formula is a diagnostic: it tells us the direction and size of the bias from a *named* omitted variable. It cannot rule out the omitted variables we have not named.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter itself notes the post-1970 slope (p ≈ 0.42) and the augmented urate coefficient (p ≈ 0.12) are not significant. The broader lesson for the policy debate: once expectations adjust, there is little long-run trade-off to exploit, which is why central banks focus on anchoring expectations.
:::

# Case 13.4 · What determines fuel economy? {#case-134 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Log-log model · 26,995 vehicles · cluster-robust standard errors]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case 13.4: a large cross-section of vehicles. Tools: elasticities from a log-log model, and why grouped data need cluster-robust standard errors.
:::

## The question: why didn't fuel economy improve more? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Data.** 26,995 vehicle models sold in the U.S., 1980–2006, from **39 manufacturers** (`AED_AUTOSMPG.DTA`). The logs come pre-computed in the data.

- `mpg`: miles per gallon (8.7 to 76.4)
- `curbwt`: weight in pounds (1,450 to 6,700)
- `hp`, `torque`: engine power and pulling force
- `year`: model year (a technology trend)
- `mfr`: manufacturer (the clustering variable)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
| Top manufacturers | Models |
|:--|--:|
| GMC | [7,979]{.key} |
| Chrysler | 4,172 |
| Ford | 3,709 |
| Toyota | 1,554 |
| Nissan | 1,079 |
| Volkswagen | 831 |
| Honda | 743 |
:::
::::

[Engines kept improving, so where did the efficiency gains go? This case links fuel economy to vehicle attributes.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Policy context: post-oil-shock demand for efficiency, CAFE fuel-economy standards, the rise of SUVs and trucks, and steady engine technology. Observations are model-level records, not sales-weighted. The panel is very unbalanced across manufacturers: GMC alone has 7,979 rows (about 30%), and the average is about 692 per manufacturer.
:::

## After 1985, the gains went into power, not mileage

![Unweighted average over the models in the data, indexed to 1980 = 100. Average MPG rose about 32% by 1985, then stayed roughly flat while horsepower nearly doubled.](figures/fig_autos_trend.png)

[From 1985 to 2006, average horsepower climbed steadily while average MPG barely moved.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Slide-only figure built from the same data (simple means by model year). 1980 → 2006: mpg 19.4 → 25.2 (index 129.5), hp 126.5 → 242.3 (index 191.5), weight 3,517 → 3,894 lb (index 110.7). These are not sales-weighted fleet averages, so read them as the attributes of the models on offer.
:::

## Why cluster by manufacturer?

Vehicles from the same manufacturer share engine platforms, engineering teams, design philosophy and testing practices. So their regression errors are **correlated within the manufacturer**.

. . .

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Default / HC1 SEs assume
- 26,995 **independent** pieces of information
- Too-small SEs, too-large $t$-stats
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Cluster-robust (CRV1) SEs allow
- any correlation **inside** each of the 39 manufacturers
- independence only **across** manufacturers
:::
::::

[With correlated errors, the effective sample size is closer to the number of clusters than to the number of rows.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.6. Ignoring within-cluster correlation understates uncertainty and leads to false rejections. CRV1 is pyfixest's standard cluster-robust estimator with a small-sample correction.
:::

## Code: log-log regression with SEs clustered by manufacturer

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6|7-9|10-11"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                    # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                       # OLS with R-style formulas
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_AUTOSMPG.DTA"
data_auto = pd.read_stata(url)              # 26,995 vehicles, 1980–2006 (logs pre-computed)
print(data_auto[["mpg", "curbwt", "hp", "torque", "year"]].describe())  # summary statistics
print(data_auto["mfr"].value_counts().head(10))                       # observations per maker
# log MPG on log HP, log weight, log torque and a linear year trend
fit_auto = pf.feols("lmpg ~ lhp + lcurbwt + ltorque + year", data=data_auto,
                    vcov={"CRV1": "mfr"})   # cluster-robust SEs by manufacturer
fit_auto.summary()                          # elasticities + clustered SEs
print(data_auto["mfr"].nunique())           # number of clusters: 39
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. The dataset already contains lmpg, lhp, lcurbwt and ltorque. The year enters in levels, so its coefficient is a proportional change in MPG per model year, holding the engine and weight fixed.
:::

## Output: weight is the dominant determinant of fuel economy {.smaller}

| Variable | Coef. | CRV1 SE | $t$ | $p$ | 95% CI |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Intercept | −20.843 | 1.988 | −10.48 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [−24.87,&nbsp;−16.82] |
| `lhp` | −0.181 | 0.065 | −2.79 | 0.008 | [−0.31,&nbsp;−0.05] |
| `lcurbwt` | [−0.562]{.key} | 0.057 | −9.94 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [−0.68,&nbsp;−0.45] |
| `ltorque` | −0.141 | 0.064 | −2.21 | 0.033 | [−0.27,&nbsp;−0.01] |
| `year` | [0.0152]{.key} | 0.0011 | 13.84 | <&nbsp;0.001 | [0.013,&nbsp;0.017] |

[N = 26,995 · SEs clustered by manufacturer (39 clusters) · $R^2 = 0.777$]{.comment}

[Weight carries the largest elasticity, and the year trend shows steady technical progress at fixed attributes.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The model explains 78% of the variation in log MPG; the rest reflects aerodynamics, transmissions, fuel type and so on. Note the CI uses the cluster-robust SE with G − 1 = 38 degrees of freedom.
:::

## Reading the elasticities: technology was "spent" on weight and power

::: {.incremental}
- **Weight −0.56**: a 1% heavier vehicle gets **≈ 0.56% lower MPG**, holding power, torque and year fixed (the largest effect)
- **Horsepower −0.18** and **torque −0.14**: ≈ 0.18% and ≈ 0.14% lower MPG per 1% increase
- **Year +0.0152**: at *fixed* weight, power and torque, MPG rises about **1.5% per model year** ($100 \times (e^{0.0152}-1) = 1.53\%$)
- **The paradox resolved**: the technology trend kept raising MPG at given attributes, while rising horsepower and weight pulled it back down
:::

[Engineers made engines more efficient every year, and buyers took the gains as more powerful (and somewhat heavier) cars.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
All elasticity statements are approximations for small changes (log-log model). The year coefficient is a semi-elasticity: 100 × 0.0152 ≈ 1.52% is the approximation; the exact proportional change is 1.53%. Policy relevance from the chapter: weight matters a great deal for CAFE compliance; lighter materials and smaller turbocharged engines are later responses (after the data end).
:::

## Clustering makes the standard errors 6–9× larger {.smaller}

| Variable | HC1 SE (ignores clusters) | CRV1 SE (by manufacturer) | Ratio |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| `lhp` | 0.0071 | 0.0651 | 9.1× |
| `lcurbwt` | 0.0080 | 0.0566 | [7.0×]{.key} |
| `ltorque` | 0.0076 | 0.0640 | 8.4× |
| `year` | 0.00017 | 0.0011 | 6.4× |

[Same coefficients; only `vcov` changes. HC1 comparison: `pf.feols("lmpg ~ lhp + lcurbwt + ltorque + year", data=data_auto, vcov="HC1")`]{.comment}

[If we ignored the clustering, every $t$-statistic would be inflated 6–9×. The torque effect ($t = 2.21$ clustered) would look like $t \approx 18.6$.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This comparison is computed for the slides (same model, same data, only the vcov differs) to quantify the chapter's statement that clustering increases the SEs. Errors within a manufacturer are strongly correlated, so the 26,995 rows contain far less independent information than their number suggests. HC1 t for ltorque: −0.1415 / 0.0076 ≈ −18.6.
:::

## Caveats: an engineering association, not a causal effect

::: {.incremental}
- **Joint choices**: weight, power and torque are chosen together by designers, so "a 1% heavier car, all else equal" is a comparison across models, not an experiment
- **Few, unbalanced clusters**: 39 manufacturers, and GMC alone is about 30% of the rows. Cluster-robust inference works best with many similar-sized clusters
- **Not sales-weighted**: every model counts equally, regardless of how many units sold
- **Overlapping engine measures**: horsepower and torque capture related engine traits, which blurs their separate effects
:::

[Within these limits, the large weight elasticity and the year trend are robust, and they tell a coherent story.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Standard caveats. With few or very unequal clusters, CRV1 SEs can still be too small; wild-cluster bootstrap is the usual remedy (not covered here). The chapter's Key Takeaways list 13.4 under "Advanced Causal Methods", but this is an observational, descriptive regression: a tool case (clustering), not a design for causation.
:::

# Act II-b · Four designs that identify causation {.divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Cases 13.5–13.8 · RCT · DiD · RD · IV]{.act}

::: {.notes}
From here on, each case asks a causal question, and each answers it with a design that supplies a credible counterfactual. The estimator is still OLS (or 2SLS); what changes is why we believe the slope.
:::

## Why a raw comparison is not a causal effect

$$\underbrace{E[Y \mid D{=}1] - E[Y \mid D{=}0]}_{\text{observed difference}} = \underbrace{E[Y_1 - Y_0 \mid D{=}1]}_{\text{effect on the treated (ATT)}} + \underbrace{E[Y_0 \mid D{=}1] - E[Y_0 \mid D{=}0]}_{\text{selection bias}}$$

[$Y_1$, $Y_0$: potential outcomes with and without treatment. We only ever observe one of them per unit. The other is the **counterfactual**.]{.comment}

[Every design in this act is a strategy for driving the **selection-bias** term to zero.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Selection bias is the difference the treated and untreated would have shown even without treatment. In observational data it is generally non-zero: people who buy generous insurance expect to need care; parties that win were already strong; rich countries can afford good institutions. This is the potential-outcomes way of saying "confounding".
:::

## Four ways to build the counterfactual {.smaller}

| Design | Where the counterfactual comes from | Case |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **RCT** | a randomly assigned control group | 13.5 RAND health insurance |
| **Difference-in-differences** | the control group's *change* over time | 13.6 South African clinics |
| **Regression discontinuity** | units just on the other side of a cutoff | 13.7 Senate elections |
| **Instrumental variables** | variation in treatment driven only by an instrument | 13.8 colonial institutions |

[Each design swaps the unverifiable "I controlled for everything" for one specific assumption you can argue about.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Keep this table in mind; the synthesis at the end of the deck adds the identifying assumption, the estimand and the main threat for each.
:::

# Case 13.5 · Does cost-sharing reduce medical spending? {#case-135 .divider background-color="#7A209F"}

[Randomized controlled trial · RAND Health Insurance Experiment · SEs clustered by family]{.act}

::: {.notes}
Case 13.5: the gold standard. Tools: regression on treatment dummies, a joint F-test with cluster-robust covariance, and the logic of random assignment.
:::

## The question: does cheaper care mean more care?

**Moral hazard**: if insurance makes care cheaper at the point of use, do people use more of it? That question drives every debate about deductibles and co-pays.

. . .

**Why observational data fail.** People *choose* their insurance:

- those who expect to be sick buy more generous plans
- income, education and health all affect both plan choice and spending

[In observational data, "generous plan → higher spending" mixes the plan's effect with **who chose it**.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Reverse causation too: health status affects insurance choice. Comparing spending across self-chosen plans therefore estimates the effect plus selection bias, with no way to separate them.
:::

## The design: random assignment to insurance plans

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**RAND Health Insurance Experiment (1974–1982)**

- families **randomly assigned** to plans
- coinsurance (the share of the bill you pay): **0% (free care)**, 25%, mixed 25/50%, 50%, 95%, or an individual deductible
- followed for 3–5 years
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Why it works**

- assignment is independent of health, income and preferences
- so the groups are identical **in expectation**
- selection bias $= 0$ **in expectation**, so the difference in means estimates the **causal effect** of each plan vs free care
:::
::::

[Randomization does not equalize the groups exactly. It makes every difference *before treatment* pure chance, which standard errors already account for.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Key Concept 13.7. Estimand: the average effect, among experiment participants, of being assigned to plan j rather than free care. Because families (not individuals) were assigned, outcomes of members of the same family are correlated, hence SEs clustered by family.
:::

## The data: year 1 of the experiment {.smaller}

| | Value |
|:--|--:|
| Person-year observations, all years | 20,203 |
| Observations used (year 1 only) | [5,639]{.key} |
| Families (clusters) in year 1 | 1,930 |
| Median annual spending (2011 \$) | \$479 |
| Largest annual spending | \$175,831 |

[Outcome `spending` = inpatient + outpatient medical spending in 2011 dollars. Plan dummies: `coins25`, `coinsmixed`, `coins50`, `coins95`, `coinsindiv`; free care is the omitted baseline.]{.comment}

[Spending is extremely skewed (median \$479, maximum \$175,831), so group means will be noisy.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The chapter follows the textbook and uses year 1 only. The heavy right tail (a few very expensive hospitalizations) is why some plan means are imprecise, especially in smaller groups.
:::

## Code: load the experiment and compare mean spending by plan

``` {.python code-line-numbers="1-3|4-6|7-8"}
!pip install -q pyfixest                    # pyfixest is not preinstalled in Colab
import pandas as pd                         # tabular data
import pyfixest as pf                       # OLS with R-style formulas
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/data-open/master/AED/AED_HEALTHINSEXP.DTA"
data_health = pd.read_stata(url)            # RAND HIE, all years (20,203 person-years)
data_health_y1 = data_health[data_health["year"] == 1]   # first year only: 5,639 obs
spending_by_plan = data_health_y1.groupby("plan")["spending"].agg(["mean", "std", "count"])
print(spending_by_plan)                     # mean, SD and size of each randomized group
```

[↗ Try it in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/notebooks/empty.ipynb){.colab-link target="_blank" data-preview-link="false"}

[With random assignment, this simple table of group means is already a causal comparison.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Self-contained. groupby("plan") gives one row per randomized arm. Note the standard deviations: the 50% plan has SD ≈ $11,644, about three times its neighbours, because of a few huge spenders.
:::

## Output: free care has the highest spending

![Mean year-1 spending by randomly assigned plan (2011 \$), with group sizes.](figures/fig_rct_means.png)

[Every cost-sharing plan spends less than free care, and the 95% plan spends about half.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Slide-only figure from the chapter's group means: free care $2,154 (n = 1,873); 25% $1,397 (639); mixed $1,702 (480); 50% $1,786 (374); individual deductible $1,607 (1,216); 95% $1,046 (1,057). The ordering is not perfectly monotone in the coinsurance rate (50% > 25%): the next slides show the 50% group is too noisy to rank.
